section.title: The Fall
section.sectionRationale: This is the hinge of the toledot of the heavens and the earth, and of the whole Bible. The harmony of chapter two ruptures: a crafty serpent, a broken command, judgment, and, in the same breath, the first promise of a rescuer.
section.thesis: Distrust of God's word fractures the good world; yet in the wreckage God seeks the guilty, promises a seed who will crush the serpent, and clothes their shame.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: the deception; God seeking the hiding pair; the serpent's fate and the first promise; the judgments; and grace in the exile.

media.alt: The tree, its fruit, and the serpent
media.caption: The tempter twists God's word beside the forbidden tree.

verses.text: Now the {{serpent|serpent}} was more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made. And he said to the woman, “Did God really say, ‘You must not eat from any tree in the garden?’”
The woman answered the serpent, “We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden,
but about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God has said, ‘You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die.’”
“You will not surely die,” the serpent told the woman.
“For God knows that in the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.
And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves.
Then the man and his wife heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the breeze of the day, and they hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.
But the LORD God called out to the man, “Where are you?”
“I heard Your voice in the garden,” he replied, “and I was afraid because I was naked; so I hid myself.”
“Who told you that you were naked?” asked the LORD God. “Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?”
And the man answered, “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”
Then the LORD God said to the woman, “What is this you have done?” “The serpent deceived me,” she replied, “and I ate.”

units.label: The serpent's fate and the first promise

verses.text: So the LORD God said to the serpent: “Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and every beast of the field! On your belly will you go, and dust you will eat, all the days of your life.
And I will put {{enmity|enmity}} between you and the woman, and between your {{seed|seed}} and her seed. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.”
To the woman He said: “I will sharply increase your pain in childbirth; in pain you will bring forth children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”

And to Adam He said: “Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground because of you; through toil you will eat of it all the days of your life.
Both thorns and thistles it will yield for you, and you will eat the plants of the field.
By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread, until you return to the ground, because out of it were you taken. For dust you are, and to dust you shall return.”

media.alt: A flaming sword guarding the way to the tree of life
media.caption: Clothed by God, yet barred from the tree of life by a flaming sword.

verses.text: And Adam named his wife {{eve|Eve}}, because she would be the mother of all the living.
And the LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and He clothed them.
Then the LORD God said, “Behold, the man has become like one of Us, knowing good and evil. And now, lest he reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever...”
Therefore the LORD God banished him from the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken.
So He drove out the man and stationed cherubim on the east side of the Garden of Eden, along with a whirling sword of flame to guard the way to the tree of life.

serpent.gloss: A serpent or snake. Here it is the crafty tempter; later Scripture identifies the ancient serpent as the devil and Satan, Revelation 12:9.

enmity.gloss: Deep hostility, open war. God Himself sets enmity between the serpent and the woman's line; the rescue of the world begins as a declaration of war on evil.

seed.gloss: Offspring or seed. The word can mean many descendants or narrow to one; across Scripture 'her seed' focuses to the one Christ who crushes the serpent, Galatians 3:16, Romans 16:20.

eve.gloss: The name Eve sounds like the Hebrew for living. In the very hour death enters, the man names his wife the mother of all the living, a small act of hope in God's promise.

basic.context: This is the hinge of the whole Bible. The good world God made is broken here. A crafty serpent tempts the woman, the man joins her, and they disobey the one command. So much of the pain in the world flows from this moment. But even here God makes a promise to put it right.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter really happened, and it explains the world we live in: why there is shame, blame, pain, and death. People debate how much is pictured in symbols, but the point stands, humanity turned from God and fell. Right in the middle, in verse 15, God promises a rescuer.
basic.originalLanguages: The tempter is the nachash, the serpent, later shown to be the devil. God sets enmity, war, between the serpent and the woman's seed, her offspring. That word seed narrows across the Bible to one person, Jesus. And the man names his wife Eve, which sounds like living, a seed of hope.
basic.typology: The garments of skin God makes point forward to sacrifice: something dies so the guilty can be covered. The promised seed who crushes the serpent points to Christ. The flaming sword that guards Eden is answered when Jesus opens the way back to the tree of life.
basic.christ: Verse 15 is the first announcement of the gospel: a descendant of the woman will crush the serpent's head, though He is struck in the doing of it. That is the cross and the resurrection. Paul says God will soon crush Satan under our feet, and Revelation shows the serpent finally defeated.
basic.god: God is holy and just: sin has real consequences. But He is also gracious: He seeks the hiding pair, He clothes them, and He promises a Saviour before He sends them out. Even His judgment is laced with mercy.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 5 says sin and death entered through Adam. Revelation 12 names the serpent as the devil. Romans 16 echoes the crushing of Satan. Revelation 22 reopens the tree of life.
basic.oneStory: This is the fall, the fracture the rest of the Bible works to heal. From the wreckage God speaks the first promise of a rescuer, and the whole story from here runs toward the seed of the woman, Jesus, who undoes what happened in the garden.

context.literary:
Genesis 3 is the second panel of the account that opened at Genesis 2:4, and it is written to be read against the first. Chapter 2 moved from dust to a living man, from one forbidden tree to a whole garden given freely, from solitude to a companion, and it ended on unashamed nakedness, Genesis 2:25. Chapter 3 runs that film backward. The companion becomes the tempter's audience, the one forbidden tree becomes the only tree that seems to matter, nakedness turns to shame, and the man who was taken from the ground is told he will return to it, verse 19.

The chapter has a deliberate symmetry. The sin travels from serpent to woman to man in verses 1 to 6. God's questioning in verses 9 to 13 runs the other way, man, then woman, with the blame passed back down to the serpent. The sentences in verses 14 to 19 then retrace the first order: serpent, woman, man. Many readers see a concentric design with the divine question of verse 9 near its centre, so that the turning point of the story is not the eating but the God who comes looking.

The narrator is sparing with motive. The serpent never commands; he only asks and asserts. The single window into the woman's mind is verse 6, three phrases that echo Genesis 2:9 and climb from appetite to the eye to ambition. The man says nothing at all until he is questioned, and then he speaks to excuse himself.

The sentences of verses 14 to 19 move into poetic parallelism, and the chapter closes in narrative again with naming, clothing and exile, verses 20 to 24, ending at the east side of the garden. That easterly direction becomes a thread through the early chapters: Cain settles east of Eden, Genesis 4:16, and the builders of Babel journey eastward, Genesis 11:2. Humanity keeps moving away from the presence it lost.
context.historical:
Israel received Genesis as the opening of the Torah, and the first hearers would have heard this chapter with the tabernacle in view. The garden is drawn in sanctuary colours. God is 'walking' there, verse 8, with the same stem of the verb that describes His presence moving through Israel's camp, Leviticus 26:12 and Deuteronomy 23:14. The way into the garden lies on the east, as the entrance to the tabernacle court did, Exodus 27:13 and Numbers 3:38. Cherubim guard it, as cherubim were worked into the veil that closed off the Most Holy Place, Exodus 26:31. To an Israelite ear, being driven from the garden sounded like being barred from the sanctuary.

The serpent was a loaded figure. Across the ancient Near East the snake carried associations of wisdom, fertility, healing and chaos, and Egyptian royal and divine imagery used it prominently. Genesis refuses to make it a god. It is one of the beasts of the field 'that the LORD God had made,' verse 1, a creature that ends the scene under a sentence, eating dust.

Other ancient stories also wrestle with lost immortality. In the Mesopotamian epic of Gilgamesh a snake steals a plant of renewed youth; in the tale of Adapa a man forfeits eternal life by refusing the food of the gods. Genesis tells a very different story. Humanity is not cheated by rival or jealous deities. The one good God gives life freely, and the human pair choose to distrust Him.

Israel would also have recognised its own shape in Adam. He was placed in a good land, given a word to keep and warned of death, disobeyed, and was sent out eastward. Israel was given Canaan and the law, warned in Deuteronomy of curse and exile, and was later carried east to Babylon. Hosea 6:7 makes the comparison in so many words: 'like Adam, have transgressed the covenant.'
context.canonical:
The rest of the Old Testament seldom names Adam, but it lives in the world this chapter creates. The curse on the ground echoes in Lamech's hope that his son would bring comfort from 'the ground that the LORD has cursed,' Genesis 5:29. The refrain 'and then he died' tolls through Genesis 5, starting with Adam himself, Genesis 5:5. Job 31:33 speaks of covering transgressions 'like Adam,' and Hosea 6:7 charges Israel with breaking covenant as he did.

The prophets reach back to Eden when they describe the future. Isaiah 51:3 and Ezekiel 36:35 promise that ruined land will become like the garden of the LORD. Isaiah 65:25 pictures peace returning among the animals, and yet 'the food of the serpent will be dust,' the sentence of Genesis 3:14 still resting on the enemy. Micah 7:17 and Psalm 72:9 describe defeated foes licking the dust, borrowing the serpent's sentence for every power that sets itself against God.

The New Testament takes the chapter up directly. Paul builds his teaching on sin, death and the two Adams on it, Romans 5:12-21 and 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 and 15:45. He uses Eve's deception as a warning to a church being led away from Christ, 2 Corinthians 11:3, and appeals to the order of the fall in 1 Timothy 2:14. Jesus calls the devil a murderer and a liar from the beginning, John 8:44, which is Genesis 3 and 4 in a sentence. Revelation names the ancient serpent outright, Revelation 12:9, and the Bible's last chapter reopens what this chapter closed: no more curse, and the tree of life standing beside the river, Revelation 22:2-3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand both themselves and their God. The chapter explains why a people who had been given every good gift and one clear word would still keep turning away. The root of sin, as Genesis tells it, is not ignorance but distrust: a willingness to believe that God is holding back something good and that His word can be edited. The serpent's first move is a question about what God said, and nearly every temptation in Israel's later story takes the same shape.

Moses also meant Israel to see that sin is never private. One act fractures every relationship at once: with God, for they hide; with each other, for they cover themselves and pass the blame; with creation, for the ground resists; and within the self, for fear and shame arrive before any sentence is spoken.

Above all, he wanted them to know how God answers. He comes to the guilty rather than waiting for them. He asks questions that invite confession. He curses the serpent and the ground but not the man and the woman themselves, and He speaks of a future offspring who will win. A people living outside the garden were meant to live by that word, to watch for that seed, and to trust the God who clothes the ashamed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records the first sin and its consequences; it does not command them. The pains, the thorns and the strained rule of verse 16 describe the world under judgment, not the world as it ought to be. That matters for application. Reading 'he will rule over you' as a mandate for husbands, rather than as a sorrowful description of how sin twists marriage, turns a curse into a charter. In the same way, easing pain in childbirth or clearing thistles from a field does not defy God. The curse is what the gospel pushes back against, not something believers must preserve.

What does carry forward is instruction by example. The chapter shows the anatomy of temptation: a question raised about God's word, His warning played down, God painted as grudging, and a desire of the eye that becomes an act of the hand. Believers are meant to recognise that pattern, as Paul does in 2 Corinthians 11:3, and to meet it as Jesus did, with the actual word of God, Matthew 4:4.

debates.question: Who or what is the serpent?

views.label: A real creature used by the devil
views.case: The text calls it one of the beasts of the field that the LORD God had made, verse 1, and its sentence is physical, going on its belly and eating dust. Yet a talking, deceiving creature that sets itself against God points beyond an animal. Later Scripture names 'that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan,' Revelation 12:9, and Jesus calls the devil a liar and murderer from the beginning, John 8:44. This has been the dominant reading in the church since the early centuries.

views.label: A literary figure for temptation or chaos
views.case: Some read the serpent as a symbol drawn from the ancient world's use of the snake, standing for the pull of forbidden wisdom or the forces of chaos, without asking whether a physical animal was present. They note that Genesis itself never names Satan and focuses on human responsibility.

views.label: A spiritual being described in serpent terms
views.case: Others take the serpent as a personal evil power appearing in this form, so that the 'dust' and 'belly' of verse 14 describe humiliation more than zoology, much as Micah 7:17 applies the same language to defeated nations.

debates.bearing: Genesis keeps the spotlight on the human choice and on God's verdict, and it never lets the tempter excuse the tempted; the woman's 'the serpent deceived me' is true but not a defence. The New Testament makes clear that a personal enemy stood behind the voice, which is why verse 15 is about a war that outlasts any snake.

debates.question: Is the seed of the woman in verse 15 humanity in general, or one individual?

views.label: A collective seed
views.case: The word zera is regularly collective, as the parallel 'your seed' for the serpent's brood shows. On this reading the verse describes the long struggle between humanity and evil, with humanity finally prevailing. Many modern scholars read it this way.

views.label: A single individual
views.case: The pronoun is singular, 'he will crush your head,' and the Greek Septuagint translators used a masculine pronoun even though their word for seed was neuter. The early church from Irenaeus onward read the verse as a promise of the Messiah, the protoevangelium.

views.label: A line that narrows to one
views.case: Genesis itself traces a chosen seed: Seth is 'another seed in place of Abel,' Genesis 4:25, then the seed of Abraham, Genesis 22:18, then David's offspring, 2 Samuel 7:12. Paul reads that line as coming to rest in one person, Galatians 3:16, while Romans 16:20 still gives the church a share in the victory.

debates.bearing: The third view gathers what is true in the first two. The verse opens a long war between two lines, but the decisive blow is struck by one, and those who belong to Him share His triumph.

debates.question: What is the woman's 'desire' in verse 16?

views.label: A longing for her husband despite the pain
views.case: Some read the desire as affection or dependence: though childbirth brings pain, she will still turn to him, and he will take advantage of it by ruling over her. Song of Songs 7:10 uses the same word of a lover's desire.

views.label: A desire to control him
views.case: The same rare word and the same pairing with 'rule' appear in Genesis 4:7, where sin's desire is for Cain and he must master it. Read in that light, verse 16 describes a new struggle for control inside marriage, which the BSB footnote reflects: 'You will desire to control your husband.'

debates.bearing: Either way the verse describes a relationship bent by sin, not God's design. The harmony of Genesis 2:23-25 gives way to rivalry and domination, and the New Testament answers it with the self-giving love of Christ for His bride, Ephesians 5:25.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter opens with a pun that English cannot keep. Genesis 2:25 ends with the pair 'naked,' arummim, and Genesis 3:1 begins with the serpent 'crafty,' arum. The words sound almost the same. The adjective arum is not always sinister; in Proverbs it describes the prudent or shrewd person, Proverbs 12:16 and 12:23. The serpent bends a capacity for shrewdness toward deceit, and the story moves from innocent nakedness to a shrewdness that leaves the pair exposed, verse 7.

The names for God shift as well. Throughout Genesis 2:4 to 3:24 the narrator speaks of 'the LORD God,' joining the covenant name to Elohim. In the dialogue of verses 1 to 5 the serpent, and then the woman, speak only of 'God.' The personal, covenant name drops out of the conversation at the very moment trust in the covenant Lord is being dissolved.

God's warning in Genesis 2:17 uses an intensive Hebrew construction, the infinitive set beside the finite verb, literally 'dying you shall die,' rendered 'you will surely die.' The generous permission of Genesis 2:16 uses the same doubled form, 'eating you may eat,' which the BSB renders 'eat freely.' The woman drops the 'freely,' adds 'or touch it,' and softens the warning to 'or you will die,' verse 3. She shrinks the gift and enlarges the prohibition. The serpent in verse 4 then repeats God's own emphatic form with a negative in front of it. He does not invent a new claim; he contradicts God word for word.

In verse 6 the tree is 'desirable,' from the root chamad, the verb of the tenth commandment, 'You shall not covet,' Exodus 20:17. The same root described every tree in the garden as 'pleasing to the eye' in Genesis 2:9. What God made to be enjoyed becomes something to be seized.

In verse 15 one verb, shuph, stands behind both blows, as the BSB footnote notes: 'he will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.' The verb is rare; Job 9:17 uses it of God crushing Job with a tempest. The difference lies not in the action but in the target, head against heel, a fatal blow against a wounding one. The Septuagint renders the subject with a masculine 'he' even though its word for seed is neuter, an early sign that the translators heard a person in the promise.

The 'desire' of verse 16, teshuqah, occurs only three times in the Old Testament: here, in Genesis 4:7, where sin's desire is for Cain and he must master it, and in Song of Songs 7:10. The word for the woman's 'pain' in childbirth, itstsabon, is the very word translated 'toil' for the man in verse 17, and it returns in Genesis 5:29. The sentence falls on both in the same currency of painful labour.

Finally, the 'garments' of verse 21 are kuttonet, the word for the tunics of Aaron's sons, Exodus 28:40, and 'He clothed them' uses the verb that describes Moses dressing the priests, Exodus 29:8 and Leviticus 8:13. And in verse 24 the cherubim are 'stationed,' from shakan, 'to dwell,' the root of mishkan, the tabernacle. The very verb of God's dwelling is used for the guard that keeps sinners out, a hint that the way back will one day run through a dwelling place.

typology.fulfillment: The fig leaves were the pair's own attempt to cover shame; the garments are God's provision, and the word and verb used are the ones later used for clothing Israel's priests, Exodus 29:8. The text does not describe a sacrifice, so the link to atonement is an inference, but a fair one: the covering came from a life taken. The escalation comes in Christ, whom believers 'put on,' Galatians 3:27 and Romans 13:14, not as a covering over a guilty self but as a new self created in true righteousness, Ephesians 4:24. The type falls short because skins covered bodies for a time; Christ's righteousness covers the person before God forever.

typology.type: The seed who crushes the serpent's head, Genesis 3:15
typology.fulfillment: The promise sets a champion from the woman's line against the serpent, taking a wound to the heel while dealing a blow to the head. In Christ the correspondence becomes exact and deeper: the wound is His death, and through that very death He destroys 'him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil,' Hebrews 2:14-15. The Son of God was revealed 'to destroy the works of the devil,' 1 John 3:8, and at the cross He disarmed the powers, Colossians 2:15. The type is still unfolding, since the final defeat awaits the day the devil is thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:10.

typology.type: Adam in the garden, the first man tested
typology.fulfillment: Paul calls Adam 'a pattern of the One to come,' Romans 5:14. Adam was tested in a garden of plenty, surrounded by good food, and failed. Jesus, tracing His line to 'Adam, the son of God,' Luke 3:38, is tested at once in a wilderness, hungry after forty days, Luke 4:1-2, and stands. Where Adam listened to a question about God's word, Jesus answered with 'It is written,' Matthew 4:4. The correspondence is real but the pattern breaks at the decisive point: Adam brought death to those in him, while Christ, the last Adam, is 'a life-giving spirit,' 1 Corinthians 15:45.

typology.type: The cherubim guarding the way to the tree of life, Genesis 3:24
typology.fulfillment: Cherubim barred the way to life, and Israel's sanctuary repeated the picture: cherubim woven into the veil, Exodus 26:31, and cherubim overshadowing the mercy seat where God met His people, Exodus 25:22. Access was real but guarded. At the death of Jesus the veil was torn from top to bottom, Matthew 27:51, and believers now enter the Most Holy Place 'by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:19-20. Jesus is Himself 'the way,' John 14:6. The escalation is that the way is not merely reopened to a garden but to the Father.

typology.type: Thorns and thistles, the sign of the cursed ground, Genesis 3:18
typology.fulfillment: Thorns are the ground's reply to human rebellion, the curse made visible in every field. The Gospels record that soldiers twisted a crown of thorns and set it on Jesus' head, Matthew 27:29. The Evangelists do not draw the line explicitly, so this is an echo rather than a declared type, but Paul states the reality it points to: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. The One who bore the curse will lift it from the whole creation, Romans 8:21 and Revelation 22:3.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by promise. Verse 15 does not name the victor, and the rest of Genesis keeps readers watching for him. Eve names Seth as 'another seed in place of Abel,' Genesis 4:25. The promise narrows to Abraham, 'through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed,' Genesis 22:18, and then to David, 'I will raise up your descendant after you,' 2 Samuel 7:12. Paul reads the whole line as coming to rest on one person: 'and to your seed,' meaning One, who is Christ, Galatians 3:16. God sent His Son, Paul says, 'born of a woman,' Galatians 4:4, a phrase that quietly recalls the woman's seed.

It leads to Christ by pattern. Luke's genealogy ends 'the son of Adam, the son of God,' Luke 3:38, and the very next scene is the temptation, Luke 4:1-2. The last Adam meets the same enemy, but in a wilderness rather than a garden, hungry rather than surrounded by fruit, and He wins where the first man lost. The serpent opened with 'Did God really say?'; Jesus answers with 'It is written,' quoting Deuteronomy 8:3, that man lives 'on every word that comes from the mouth of God,' Matthew 4:4.

It leads to Christ by contrast, and the contrasts run deep. Adam hid among the trees; Christ was hung on a tree and bore our sins there, 1 Peter 2:24. Adam blamed the woman God gave him; Christ 'loved the church and gave Himself up for her,' Ephesians 5:25. Adam reached for what was forbidden; Christ in a garden across the Kidron, John 18:1, prayed 'not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39. Adam wore thorns as the fruit of his sin; Christ wore them as a crown, Matthew 27:29. Adam was sent from the garden to die; Christ was laid in a garden tomb, John 19:41, and rose, and was mistaken for the gardener, John 20:15.

The heel wound matters too. The promise never pictured a victory without cost. Hebrews says He shared our flesh and blood 'so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death,' Hebrews 2:14. The strike to the heel and the crushing of the head happen in the same act.

A word of caution keeps the reading honest. Not every detail of Genesis 3 is a picture of Jesus; the fig leaves, the trees and the cherubim are not coded messages. The links above rest on the New Testament's own use of the chapter, and on the promise that the chapter itself sets ringing. What the chapter supplies is the problem Christ solves and the first word of the solution. He is the one who tells a dying thief, 'today you will be with Me in Paradise,' Luke 23:43, and who promises the one who overcomes the right 'to eat from the tree of life,' Revelation 2:7.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows about God is that His word is the axis of everything. The serpent's strategy is to make God's speech doubtful and God's character suspect, as though the Giver of every tree were jealous of His creatures. The chapter vindicates God on both counts. His word proves true: the pair begin to die that day, cut off from the tree of life, and the refrain of Genesis 5 carries it out, beginning with 'and then he died,' Genesis 5:5. And His character proves generous, for the only thing He withheld was the one thing that would harm them.

He is the God who seeks. His questions, 'Where are you?' and 'Who told you that you were naked?' and 'What is this you have done?', are not requests for information. The God who knows all things asks so that the guilty will speak the truth, just as He later asks Cain, 'Where is your brother Abel?' Genesis 4:9, and Elijah, 'What are you doing here?' 1 Kings 19:9. Notice that He asks the man and the woman, but He puts no question to the serpent. He does not negotiate with evil. He simply sentences it.

He is just, and His justice is measured and ordered. Each party is addressed in turn, and each sentence touches the sphere of life that belonged to them, the serpent's standing, the woman's bearing of children and her marriage, the man's work of the ground. Yet the word 'cursed' falls on the serpent and on the ground, not on the man and woman themselves. Judgment is real, but it is bounded.

He holds justice and mercy together without letting go of either. Childbearing continues under the sentence, which means the promised seed can still come. Work continues, though in toil, so life goes on. God clothes them before He sends them out, and even the exile guards them from living forever in a fallen state, verse 22.

He is holy. The cherubim and the flaming sword say that sinners cannot simply walk back into His presence. Yet the same cherubim later stand over the mercy seat, where God promises, 'I will meet with you there,' Exodus 25:22. The guard at the door of Eden becomes the throne of atonement. Verse 22 also records God speaking as 'one of Us,' as in Genesis 1:26 and 11:7, a plurality within the one God that later revelation fills out.

For worship, the chapter teaches us to hear God's questions as grace. The right response to 'Where are you?' is not to hide or to blame but to come out and confess, and to trust that the God who asks is the God who has already promised a Rescuer and made clothes for the naked.

crossReferences.note: The command the serpent misquotes. God's word began with generosity, 'You may eat freely from every tree,' and set one limit with a clear warning. Genesis 3:1 turns that around into 'You must not eat from any tree,' making God sound stingy. Reading the two side by side shows exactly how the lie was built.

The only other place in Genesis where the rare word for desire appears, again paired with the verb rule. Sin crouches at Cain's door, desiring him, and he must master it. The echo of Genesis 3:16 shows how quickly the fracture of the garden spreads to the next generation, ending in murder, Genesis 4:8.

The tempter who questioned God's word in the garden meets Jesus in the wilderness. Three times Jesus answers with Scripture, beginning with Deuteronomy 8:3. The last Adam succeeds in harder circumstances, hungry and alone, where the first Adam failed in plenty. It is the fall of Genesis 3 reversed in the life of one Man.

Paul fears the Corinthians will be led astray just as Eve was deceived by the serpent's cunning. He treats Genesis 3 as the template of every deception that draws believers from simple devotion to Christ, which is why false teaching often begins, like the serpent, by reshaping what God has said.

Jesus calls the devil 'a murderer from the beginning' and 'the father of lies.' Both titles reach back to the opening chapters of Genesis: the lie of Genesis 3:4, 'You will not surely die,' and the murder that followed in Genesis 4. Jesus identifies the voice behind the serpent.

Explains how the crushing of Genesis 3:15 happens. The Son shares our flesh and blood so that through His own death He destroys the one who holds the power of death, freeing people enslaved by fear of it. The wounded heel and the crushed head are one event.

Paul argues that the promise to Abraham's seed points to one person, Christ. That same singular seed runs back to Genesis 3:15, where the offspring of the woman is spoken of as 'he.' The promise that begins in the garden narrows through Abraham to its single fulfilment.

Paul describes the creation 'subjected to futility' by God in hope, groaning 'in the pains of childbirth.' The language gathers up the cursed ground of Genesis 3:17-18 and the pain of 3:16 and gives them a future: creation will be set free when God's children are revealed.

The cherubim of Genesis 3:24 reappear woven into the tabernacle veil, Exodus 26:31, marking the way to God as closed. Hebrews announces that Jesus has opened a new and living way through the curtain of His body, so that believers may enter the Most Holy Place with confidence.

In Isaiah's vision of new heavens and a new earth the wolf and lamb feed together, yet 'the food of the serpent will be dust.' The curse of Genesis 3:14 is the one sentence that remains in the renewed world. Every other enmity is healed, but the enemy stays defeated.

Paul promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under the feet of the Roman believers. The verb picks up the imagery of Genesis 3:15, but the victory Christ won is now shared by His people, so the church stands on the serpent's head in Him as it resists false teachers.

The Bible closes by undoing this chapter point by point. The tree of life stands open beside the river, there is no longer any curse, and God's servants 'will see His face.' The pair who hid from God's presence in Genesis 3:8 are answered by a people who look on Him without fear.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 1 closed with God looking on all He had made and finding it 'very good,' Genesis 1:31, and Genesis 2 ended with a man and woman naked and unashamed before Him and each other. Genesis 3 answers the question every reader of the Bible eventually asks: if the world began like that, why is it like this? The answer is not a flaw in the making but a rupture in trust. Everything that goes wrong afterward traces back to this one act of distrust.

The effects unfold at once. In chapter 4 a brother murders a brother; in chapter 5 death becomes the refrain of every life; by Genesis 6:5 the thoughts of the human heart are 'altogether evil all the time.' The ground stays cursed, and the story keeps moving east, away from the presence of God.

But chapter 3 also sets up the whole rescue. The promise of verse 15 becomes the thread by which the rest of Genesis is sewn together, as the chosen seed passes from Seth to Noah to Abraham. When God calls Abraham, the word curse gives way to blessing: 'all the families of the earth will be blessed through you,' Genesis 12:3. Israel is then given what Adam lost in picture form, a land, a sanctuary where God walks among His people, and cherubim over the place of atonement. Yet Israel repeats Adam's failure and is driven east into exile, showing that the seed must be more than a nation.

The story comes to rest in Christ, the last Adam, who is tested and does not fall, who is wounded and in that wound crushes the enemy, who bears the curse and opens the way through the veil. His people share His victory, Romans 16:20, and live now as those clothed with Him while the creation still groans.

The new creation is Genesis 3 undone. There will be 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4, the pain of Genesis 3:16 gone for good. There will be no longer any curse, the tree of life will bear fruit every month, and God's people 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:2-4. The couple who hid among the trees are answered by a people who live in the light of His presence, and the garden becomes a city where God Himself dwells with humanity, Revelation 21:3.

sermon.title: Paradise Lost (Genesis 3:8 to 24)
sermon.why: Keller works through the fall to answer what went wrong with the human race and how God begins to put it right, drawing out the grace and the first promise of the gospel in this chapter.

quiz.q: How did the serpent first lead the woman into sin?

options.text: By casting doubt on God's word and God's goodness, 'Did God really say'.
options.note: Temptation begins by twisting and doubting what God has said.

options.text: By offering fruit that looked good to eat.
options.note: The fruit's appeal is real, but the root was doubting God's word.

options.text: By forcing her to eat against her will.
options.note: She was deceived and chose; she was not forced.

options.text: By proving that God had lied.
options.note: God had not lied; the serpent lied, and the warned death came.

quiz.q: What is the first promise of the gospel in this chapter?

options.text: Genesis 3:15, a seed of the woman will crush the serpent's head.
options.note: This is the protoevangelium, the first announcement of Christ's victory.

options.text: That God would clothe them with garments of skin.
options.note: A true grace and a shadow of atonement, but the explicit promise is verse 15.

options.text: That childbirth would still continue.
options.note: A mercy within judgment, but not the gospel promise.

options.text: That there is no real hope after the fall.
options.note: The chapter is full of hope; God promises a rescuer.

quiz.q: How does God show grace even in judgment?

options.text: He seeks them, promises a Saviour, and clothes their shame before sending them out.
options.note: Mercy runs through the whole scene.

options.text: He lets them live rather than killing them at once.
options.note: True, but it understates the depth of grace, the promise and the covering.

options.text: He removes all the consequences of their sin.
options.note: He does not remove the consequences; sin is judged, yet mercy is shown.

options.text: He shows no grace at all, only anger.
options.note: The chapter is threaded with grace: seeking, promise, and covering.

quiz.q: Who is the seed of the woman, ultimately?

options.text: Jesus Christ, who crushes the serpent through His death and resurrection.
options.note: The New Testament identifies the seed as Christ, Galatians 3 and Romans 16:20.

options.text: The line of faithful people descended from Eve.
options.note: The seed runs through a line, but it narrows to one, Christ.

options.text: Any person who resists evil.
options.note: This misses that the promise centres on one appointed rescuer.

options.text: No one; it is only a symbol.
options.note: Scripture treats it as a real promise fulfilled in Jesus.

quiz.q: What went wrong in the fall, at its heart?

options.text: Humanity distrusted God and grasped to be like God apart from Him.
options.note: The root of sin is distrust and self-rule against God.

options.text: They broke a rule about a tree.
options.note: True on the surface, but the deeper issue was distrust of God Himself.

options.text: They simply made an honest mistake.
options.note: It was disobedience and distrust, not a mere slip.

options.text: God set them up to fail.
options.note: God provided abundantly and warned truthfully; the choice was theirs.

questions: Temptation still begins with 'Did God really say'. Where are you being tempted to doubt God's word or His goodness right now?
Adam blamed Eve, and Eve blamed the serpent. Where are you hiding, or shifting blame, instead of coming honestly to God?
God came seeking with 'Where are you'. How does it change things to know that God pursues sinners rather than waiting for them to clean themselves up first?
God covered their shame with garments He provided. What are you using to cover your own shame, and what would it mean to receive God's covering in Christ instead?
The crushing of the serpent is fulfilled in Jesus. How does knowing that evil is already defeated help you face temptation and suffering this week?

translationNotes.note: The same Hebrew root can be rendered crush, bruise, or strike, and it appears for both the head and the heel. The wordplay holds together decisive victory over the serpent and real cost to the rescuer.
Your desire will be for your husband can also be rendered you will desire to control your husband; either way it describes the conflict that now marks the relationship.
Eve sounds like the Hebrew for living or life; naming her so is an act of hope spoken right after the sentence of death.
